children.title: 1.1. Counting Principle
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 1. Combinatorics/1.1. Counting Principle
children.summary: This page is from Chapter 1 of a document on Combinatorics, specifically section 1.1 covering the Counting Principle. It defines the Basic Counting Principle (multiplying possibilities for sequential experiments) and introduces the 'box method' as a visualization tool. The text includes four examples demonstrating how to apply this principle: selecting a teacher and student, forming a subcommittee with specific class requirements, calculating license plate combinations, and determining possible functions.

children.title: 1.2. Permutations
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 1. Combinatorics/1.2. Permutations
children.summary: This page, titled '1.2. Permutations', explains the mathematical concept of permutations and provides several examples. It defines a permutation as an ordered arrangement of objects and presents the formula for n distinct objects (n!). The text includes specific examples involving arranging letters, books on a shelf, and players from different countries, covering cases with repetitions.

children.title: 1.3. Combinations
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 1. Combinatorics/1.3. Combinations
children.summary: This section introduces combinations, defined as the number of ways to select r objects from a total of n where order does not matter. It provides the general formula for 'n choose r' and defines these values as binomial coefficients. The text includes several examples involving committees and party invitations, proves the Binomial Theorem using combinatorial logic, and demonstrates Pascal's Identity with a proof based on whether a specific person (the President) is included in a committee.

children.title: 1.4. Multinomial Coefficients
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 1. Combinatorics/1.4. Multinomial Coefficients
children.summary: This page, titled '1.4. Multinomial Coefficients', explains the concept of multinomial coefficients through several examples and a general formula. It details how to divide objects into distinct groups (like committees or police officers) and calculate the number of ways to do so using factorials. The page also covers related combinatorial problems involving indistinguishable items, such as arranging flags on a pole and distributing balls into boxes.

sections.title: Chapter 2. Axioms of Probability
sections.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 2. Axioms of Probability

children.title: 2.1. Sample Space and Events
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 2. Axioms of Probability/2.1. Sample Space and Events
children.summary: This section defines the fundamental concepts of sample space (S) and events in probability theory. It provides examples of sample spaces for various experiments, such as rolling dice or tossing coins. The text then defines an event as a subset of the sample space and explains set operations including union, intersection, and complement. It also covers properties like De Morgan's Law, the empty set, and the concept of disjoint (mutually exclusive) events.

children.title: 2.2. Axioms of Probability
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 2. Axioms of Probability/2.2. Axioms of Probability
children.summary: This section introduces the axioms of probability as a formal framework, moving beyond the concept of relative frequency. It defines three core axioms: non-negativity (probability is between 0 and 1), normalization (the probability of the sample space S is 1), and countable additivity for disjoint events. The text provides examples using coin tosses and dice rolls to illustrate these concepts. It then presents Proposition 1, which lists several derived rules of probability, such as the probability of an empty set being zero and the formula for the union of two events. The section concludes with proofs for these propositions and a practical example involving the probabilities of UConn Basketball winning games against Kentucky.

children.title: 2.3. Equally Likely Outcomes
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 2. Axioms of Probability/2.3. Equally Likely Outcomes
children.summary: This section, titled 'Equally Likely Outcomes', introduces the concept of probability spaces with finitely many points that have equal probabilities. It provides the formula for calculating the probability of an event in such a space and illustrates its application through several examples. These examples include rolling dice to get a specific sum, drawing colored balls from a bowl, forming a committee from a group of men and women, and drawing colored balls from an urn. The section also covers probability problems related to poker hands (4 of a kind, straight, full house) and the classic Birthday Problem.

children.title: 3.1. Independent Events
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 3. Independence/3.1. Independent Events

children.title: Example (A variation of Gambler's ruin)
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 3. Independence/3.1. Independent Events/Example (A variation of Gambler's ruin)
children.summary: This section presents a variation of the Gambler's ruin problem where an individual can go arbitrarily far into debt. It seeks to find the probability p(x) of reaching $200 starting from x. The text analyzes two methods: first, by observing that the slope of the linear function cannot be negative or positive (as it would violate probability bounds), concluding p(x) is constant and equal to 1; second, by computing the limit as the lower bound M approaches infinity, also yielding a probability of 1.

children.title: Example:
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 3. Independence/3.1. Independent Events/Example:
children.summary: This section presents two examples related to independent events. The first example is a variation of the Gambler's ruin problem, calculating the probability of reaching a target amount ($200) starting from debt, concluding that the probability is 1. The second example calculates the probability of rolling exactly four twos in ten dice rolls, introducing the concept of Bernoulli trials and the Binomial distribution formula.

children.title: Conditional Probability and Independence
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 3. Independence/3.1. Independent Events/Conditional Probability and Independence
children.summary: This page is from Chapter 4, titled 'Conditional Probability and Independence,' and covers section 4.1 on Conditional Probabilities. It introduces the concept through a scenario involving men and women smokers, defines the mathematical formula for conditional probability P(E | F), and discusses independence. The text concludes with an example problem regarding rolling two dice to calculate probabilities.

sections.title: Chapter 4. Conditional Probability and Independence
sections.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 4. Conditional Probability and Independence

children.title: 4.1. Conditional Probabilities
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 4. Conditional Probability and Independence/4.1. Conditional Probabilities

children.title: Example5:
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 4. Conditional Probability and Independence/4.1. Conditional Probabilities/Example5:
children.summary: The section titled 'Example 5' presents a probability problem involving an urn containing 5 white balls and 7 black balls. The experiment involves drawing 3 balls with replacement, where each drawn ball is returned to the urn along with an additional ball of the same color (a Polya Urn scheme). Part (a) calculates the probability of drawing 3 white balls in succession, resulting in the calculation P(3 white balls) = (5/12) * (6/13) * (7/14).

children.title: 4.2. Bayes's Formula
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 4. Conditional Probability and Independence/4.2. Bayes's Formula
children.summary: This section introduces Bayes's Formula by first deriving the Law of Total Probability. It then presents five examples to illustrate its application: calculating accident proneness in insurance, determining HIV test accuracy, finding the probability of a student being a woman given an 'A' grade, analyzing defective iPhones from different factory machines, and solving a multiple-choice test problem.

sections.title: Chapter 5. Random Variables
sections.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 5. Random Variables

children.title: 5.1. Random Variables
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 5. Random Variables/5.1. Random Variables
children.summary: This section defines a random variable as a function that maps outcomes of an experiment to numerical values. It provides several examples, including tossing a coin, rolling a die, and counting successes in trials, to illustrate how different experiments can be modeled by random variables (denoted by capital letters like X or Y). The text also discusses the range of possible values a random variable can attain. The second page continues this discussion by assigning probabilities to the specific values of a random variable derived from tossing a coin three times, demonstrating that the sum of these probabilities equals 1.

children.title: 5.2. Discrete Random Variables
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 5. Random Variables/5.2. Discrete Random Variables
children.summary: This page, titled '5.2. Discrete Random Variables', defines discrete random variables and their probability mass function (pmf). It outlines the properties of a pmf, including that probabilities must be between 0 and 1 and sum to 1. The page provides examples, such as a coin toss modeled by a bar graph, and details calculations for a Poisson distribution with parameter λ.

children.title: 5.3. Expected Value
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 5. Random Variables/5.3. Expected Value
children.summary: The section titled '5.3. Expected Value' defines the concept of expectation for a random variable X with a probability mass function p(x) using the formula E[X] = Σ xp(x). It provides three examples: calculating the expected value for a coin flip (Example 1), a fair die roll (Example 2), and the number of tornadoes in Connecticut per year (Example 3). The text also reviews infinite geometric series and their derivatives to solve the third example, which involves an infinite sum.

children.title: 5.4. The C.D.F.
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 5. Random Variables/5.4. The C.D.F.
children.summary: This section defines the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF), denoted as F(x) = P(X ≤ x). It provides an example of calculating the CDF for a discrete random variable representing the number of heads in three coin flips, showing both the step function formula and its graph. The section then lists key properties of the CDF, such as being non-decreasing and right-continuous. Finally, it presents Proposition 3, which relates probabilities to limits of the CDF, and includes a proof for part (a) along with another example demonstrating how to compute specific probabilities using the CDF.

children.title: 5.5. Expected Value of Sums of Random Variables
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 5. Random Variables/5.5. Expected Value of Sums of Random Variables
children.summary: This section introduces a formal definition for the expected value of a random variable, denoted as E[X], which sums over the sample space S. It provides an example to illustrate this definition and proves that it is equivalent to the standard definition based on the range of values. The section then uses this definition to prove the linearity of expectation (Theorem 5), showing that E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] and E[aX] = aE[X].

children.title: 5.6. Expectation of a Function of a Random Variable
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 5. Random Variables/5.6. Expectation of a Function of a Random Variable
children.summary: This section explains how to calculate the expected value of a function of a random variable, $g(X)$. It introduces Theorem 6, which provides the formula for this calculation: $\mathbb{E}[g(X)] = \sum g(x_i)p(x_i)$. A proof is provided showing that summing over the values of $Y=g(X)$ is equivalent to summing over the values of $X$ weighted by their probabilities. The section also defines the mean ($\mu = \mathbb{E}X$) as the first moment and generalizes this to the $n$th moment ($\mathbb{E}X^n$).

children.title: 5.7. Variance
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 5. Random Variables/5.7. Variance
children.summary: This section defines variance as a measure of the spread of values in a random variable, contrasting it with expectation. It provides the formal definition Var(X) = E[(X - μ)²] and derives an alternate formula, Var(X) = E[X²] - (E[X])². The section includes an example calculating the variance of a fair die roll and concludes with Proposition 7, which states the property Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X), followed by the definition of standard deviation.

sections.title: Chapter 6. Some Discrete Distributions
sections.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 6. Some Discrete Distributions

children.title: 6.1. Bernouli and Binomial Random Variables
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 6. Some Discrete Distributions/6.1. Bernouli and Binomial Random Variables
children.summary: This section defines Bernoulli and Binomial random variables. It details the probability mass function, mean, and variance for a Bernoulli distribution. For the Binomial distribution, it provides the formula, interprets it as the number of successes in independent trials, and derives its mean and variance using properties of independent Bernoulli trials. The section concludes with two applied examples: one calculating the probability of fewer than 3 hurricanes in a 20-year period, and another calculating the probability that a basketball player makes at least 2 out of 10 free throws.

children.title: 6.2. The Poisson Distribution
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 6. Some Discrete Distributions/6.2. The Poisson Distribution
children.summary: This section introduces the Poisson distribution, defining it by its probability mass function p_X(i) = e^(-λ) * (λ^i / i!) for a parameter λ > 0. It provides examples of phenomena that follow this distribution, such as misprints on a page or telephone calls in a day. The section then derives the mean and variance of the Poisson distribution, showing both are equal to λ. It also discusses the relationship between the Binomial and Poisson distributions, stating that a Binomial(n, p) distribution can be approximated by a Poisson(λ) distribution when n is large and p is small, with λ = np. Several numerical examples are provided to illustrate these concepts.

children.title: 6.3. Other Discrete Distributions
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 6. Some Discrete Distributions/6.3. Other Discrete Distributions

children.title: Negative Binomial(Need to know for Actuarial Exam):
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 6. Some Discrete Distributions/6.3. Other Discrete Distributions/Negative Binomial(Need to know for Actuarial Exam):
children.summary: This section defines the Negative Binomial distribution, describing an experiment where independent trials are performed until a total of r successes are accumulated. It provides the probability mass function for X (the number of trials required), notation X ~ NegativeBinomial(r,p), and formulas for the Mean (r/p) and Variance (r(1-p)/p^2). It also notes that the Geometric distribution is a special case where r=1. Finally, it presents an example problem calculating the expected value of throwing a die until the outcome '1' occurs 4 times.

children.title: Hypergeometric Distribution(Need to know for Actuarial Exam):
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 6. Some Discrete Distributions/6.3. Other Discrete Distributions/Hypergeometric Distribution(Need to know for Actuarial Exam):
children.summary: This section introduces the Hypergeometric Distribution, a discrete probability distribution used when sampling without replacement. It defines an experiment where a sample of size n is chosen from an urn containing N balls (m white and N-m black). The text provides the probability mass function for X (the number of white balls selected), notation (X ~ Hypergeometric(n, N, m)), and formulas for the Mean (E[X] = nm/N) and Variance.

children.title: Continuous Random Variables
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 6. Some Discrete Distributions/6.3. Other Discrete Distributions/Continuous Random Variables
children.summary: The section defines a continuous random variable and its probability density function (pdf). It outlines the two necessary properties for a function to be a pdf: non-negativity and an integral over all real numbers equaling 1. The text also provides key properties of continuous distributions, such as the probability of a single point being zero, and gives examples of continuous variables like time, stock prices, and height. Finally, it presents an example problem calculating a constant 'c' for a given piecewise pdf.

sections.title: Chapter 7. Continuous Random Variables
sections.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 7. Continuous Random Variables

children.title: 7.1. Intro to continuous R.V
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 7. Continuous Random Variables/7.1. Intro to continuous R.V
children.summary: This section introduces continuous random variables (R.V.) by defining a continuous distribution via a probability density function (pdf), denoted as f(x). It outlines the two key properties of a pdf: non-negativity and that its integral over all real numbers equals 1. The text explains that for continuous variables, the probability of any single point is zero, and probabilities are calculated as the area under the curve. Examples include time to finish an exam, stock prices, and student height. The section provides examples of calculating constants for valid pdfs, finding cumulative distribution functions (c.d.f.), and using the c.d.f. to find probabilities. A key relationship highlighted is that the derivative of the CDF is the PDF.

children.title: 7.2. Expectation and Variance
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 7. Continuous Random Variables/7.2. Expectation and Variance
children.summary: This section defines the expectation (mean) for continuous random variables using integrals and provides examples of its calculation. It presents Theorem 9 on the linearity of expectation, a proposition for finding the expected value of a function of a random variable, and Lemma 10 for non-negative random variables. The section also introduces variance, defining it with two equivalent formulas and stating its properties. Several examples are worked through to calculate expectations and variances for specific probability density functions.

children.title: 7.3. The uniform Random Variable
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 7. Continuous Random Variables/7.3. The uniform Random Variable
children.summary: This page, titled '7.3. The uniform Random Variable', defines a continuous random variable that is uniformly distributed on an interval [a, b]. It provides the probability density function (PDF) and cumulative distribution function (CDF) for this distribution. Additionally, it presents Example 1, which derives the mean and variance of a Uniform(a, b) random variable through integration.

children.title: 7.4. More practice
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 7. Continuous Random Variables/7.4. More practice
children.summary: The section titled '7.4. More practice' presents a set of exercises based on a given probability density function (p.d.f.), f(x) = 9e^(-9x) for x ≥ 0. The problems involve setting up integrals to find the cumulative distribution function F_X(x) and various probabilities, such as P(1 < X < 5), P(X > 3), and P(X < 2).

sections.title: Chapter 8. Normal Distributions
sections.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 8. Normal Distributions

children.title: 8.1. The normal distribution
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 8. Normal Distributions/8.1. The normal distribution

children.title: Summary of the normal distribution:
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 8. Normal Distributions/8.1. The normal distribution/Summary of the normal distribution:
children.summary: This page, titled '8.1. THE NORMAL DISTRIBUTION', presents a mathematical proof for Theorem 11 regarding the mean and variance of a normal random variable $X$. It details the derivation using probability density functions and cumulative distribution functions. The bottom section summarizes key properties of the normal distribution, including the definition of the standard normal random variable $Z$, the concept of Z-scores, and the formula for the cumulative distribution function $ ext{Phi}(x)$.

children.title: THEOREM 12. If X ~ N(μ, σ) then
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 8. Normal Distributions/8.1. The normal distribution/THEOREM 12. If X ~ N(μ, σ) then
children.summary: This section presents Theorem 12 regarding the standardization of a normal distribution variable X ~ N(μ, σ). It provides two detailed examples demonstrating how to calculate probabilities using this theorem: Example 1 calculates P(1 ≤ X ≤ 4) for a specific normal distribution, and Example 2 determines the standard deviation given a probability condition. An extra example is introduced at the end. The content continues on the next page with the solution to the extra example and introduces the '68-95-99.7 Rule' (Empirical Rule), which describes the percentage of data within one, two, and three standard deviations of the mean, illustrated by a bell curve graph.

children.title: Normal approximations to the binomial
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 8. Normal Distributions/8.1. The normal distribution/Normal approximations to the binomial
children.summary: The section titled 'Normal approximations to the binomial' introduces Theorem 13, which states that a standardized binomial random variable converges in distribution to a standard normal variable as n approaches infinity. It explains how to approximate probabilities for a binomial variable S_n using the normal distribution by standardizing with mean μ = np and standard deviation σ = √(np(1-p)). The text highlights that since S_n is discrete while the normal distribution is continuous, one must use inequalities rather than equalities. It provides a convention for estimating P(S_n = i) by integrating over the interval (i - 1/2, i + 1/2). The section concludes with an example setup involving tossing a fair coin 100 times.

sections.title: Chapter 9. Normal approximations to the binomial
sections.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 9. Normal approximations to the binomial

children.title: 9.1. The normal approximates Binomial
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 9. Normal approximations to the binomial/9.1. The normal approximates Binomial
children.summary: This section explains the normal approximation to the binomial distribution. It presents Theorem 13, which states that for a large number of trials (n), the standardized binomial random variable converges to a standard normal distribution. The text highlights the distinction between discrete binomial variables and continuous normal variables, introducing the concept of continuity correction (e.g., approximating P(S_n = i) as P(i - 0.5 < S_n < i + 0.5)) to handle this difference. An example is provided involving tossing a fair coin 100 times to demonstrate how to calculate probabilities using the normal approximation.

sections.title: Chapter 10. Some continuous distributions
sections.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 10. Some continuous distributions

children.title: 10.1. Exponential Random Variables
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 10. Some continuous distributions/10.1. Exponential Random Variables
children.summary: This section defines the exponential random variable, providing its probability density function (pdf), cumulative distribution function (cdf), mean, and variance. It explains how to interpret the variable as the time until a specific event occurs and illustrates this with examples involving phone call lengths and earthquake timing. The section also introduces the memoryless property of the exponential distribution, proving it mathematically and applying it to an example about the lifespan of an iPhone. Finally, it presents a problem concerning the probability of accidents for 'BAD drivers' over a period of days.

children.title: 10.2. Other Continuous Distributions
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 10. Some continuous distributions/10.2. Other Continuous Distributions
children.summary: The section titled '10.2. Other Continuous Distributions' introduces three specific probability distributions: the Gamma Distribution, the Weibull Distribution, and the Cauchy Distribution. For each distribution, it provides the mathematical definition of its probability density function (PDF), key parameters, and relevant properties or applications. The Gamma distribution is defined with parameters α and λ, including its relation to the Chi-Squared distribution. The Weibull distribution is noted for its utility in engineering contexts regarding object lifetimes. The Cauchy distribution is highlighted for having an undefined mean, with a derivation provided to demonstrate this property.

children.title: 10.3. The distribution function of a Random variable
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 10. Some continuous distributions/10.3. The distribution function of a Random variable

children.title: Example3
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 10. Some continuous distributions/10.3. The distribution function of a Random variable/Example3
children.summary: The section titled 'Example3' presents a problem where X is uniformly distributed on (0, 1] and Y = -ln(X). The goal is to find the probability density function (pdf) of Y. The solution begins by recalling the pdf of X, then proceeds to derive the cumulative distribution function (cdf) of Y in terms of F_X, followed by taking the derivative to obtain the pdf of Y. The final result shows that Y follows an exponential distribution with parameter 1.

children.title: PROPOSITION 15. Suppose g : R -> R is a strictly increasing function, then the inverse g^-1 exists and g(x) <= y implies x <= g^-1(y).
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 10. Some continuous distributions/10.3. The distribution function of a Random variable/PROPOSITION 15. Suppose g : R -> R is a strictly increasing function, then the inverse g^-1 exists and g(x) <= y implies x <= g^-1(y).
children.summary: This page from a mathematics textbook (page 73) covers the distribution function of a random variable. It includes an exercise regarding the Gamma distribution and a detailed example problem involving an Actuarial Exam question about the time a manufacturing system is out of operation. The solution demonstrates how to find the density function for a cost variable Y derived from the time T, using cumulative distribution functions and derivatives. The page concludes with Proposition 15 concerning strictly increasing functions and their inverses.

children.title: Multivariate distributions
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 10. Some continuous distributions/10.3. The distribution function of a Random variable/Multivariate distributions
children.summary: This page is from Chapter 11 of a textbook, covering 'Multivariate distributions' and specifically section 11.1 on 'Joint distribution functions'. It defines joint probability mass functions (pmf) for discrete variables and cumulative distribution functions (cdf), followed by an example involving rolling two 3-sided dice to calculate the joint pmf of the maximum value and the sum. The page concludes with a brief introduction to continuous random variables and their joint probability density function.

sections.title: Chapter 11. Multivariate distributions
sections.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 11. Multivariate distributions

children.title: 11.1. Joint distribution functions
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 11. Multivariate distributions/11.1. Joint distribution functions

children.title: Example2:
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 11. Multivariate distributions/11.1. Joint distribution functions/Example2:
children.summary: This section, titled 'Example2', presents a multi-part problem involving a joint probability density function (pdf) for two random variables, X and Y. The example first determines the constant 'c' that normalizes the pdf. It then calculates the probability P(X < Y) using two different methods of integration (Top-Bottom and Right-Left). Subsequently, it sets up the integral for P(X > 1, Y < 1), finds the marginal density f_X(x), and finally calculates the expected value E[X].

children.title: 11.2. Independent Random Variables
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 11. Multivariate distributions/11.2. Independent Random Variables
children.summary: This section defines independent random variables for both discrete and continuous cases, stating that independence holds when the joint probability mass function (pmf) or probability density function (pdf) factors into the product of the marginal functions. It presents Theorem 16, which formalizes this condition, and provides four examples demonstrating how to check for independence by calculating marginals and verifying the factorization, including a case where the domain is not rectangular.

children.title: 11.3. Sums of independent Random Variables(*)
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 11. Multivariate distributions/11.3. Sums of independent Random Variables(*)
children.summary: The section titled 'Sums of independent Random Variables' derives the cumulative distribution function (CDF) and probability density function (PDF) for the sum of two independent random variables. It presents key facts regarding the sums of independent normal random variables, including properties of linear combinations, and provides a detailed example calculating probabilities related to the average grades of two students, Tyler and Habib. The section also covers the relationship between standard normal variables and the Chi-squared distribution, as well as the property that the sum of independent Poisson random variables is itself a Poisson random variable.

children.title: 11.4. Conditional Distributions- Discrete(*)
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 11. Multivariate distributions/11.4. Conditional Distributions- Discrete(*)
children.summary: This page presents Section 11.4 on Conditional Distributions for Discrete Random Variables. It defines the conditional probability mass function (pmf) and cumulative distribution function (cdf), states a fact regarding independence, and provides 'Example1' which includes a table of joint pmf values for variables X and Y. The example demonstrates how to compute specific conditional probabilities and concludes by determining that the variables are not independent.

children.title: 11.5. Conditional Distributions- Continuous(*)
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 11. Multivariate distributions/11.5. Conditional Distributions- Continuous(*)
children.summary: This page presents Section 11.5 on Conditional Distributions for continuous random variables. It defines the conditional probability density function (pdf) and cumulative distribution function (cdf), states a fact regarding independent variables, and provides a worked example calculating the conditional pdf of X given Y=y based on a specific joint pdf.

children.title: 11.6. Joint PDF of functions
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 11. Multivariate distributions/11.6. Joint PDF of functions
children.summary: This section, titled 'Joint PDF of functions', outlines the methodology for determining the joint probability density function (PDF) of new random variables derived from existing ones. It details a three-step process: calculating the Jacobian determinant, solving for the original variables in terms of the new ones, and applying the transformation formula to find the new joint PDF. The section includes three illustrative examples covering linear transformations, transformations involving independent normal distributions, and non-linear transformations.

children.title: 12.1. Expectation of Sums of R.V.
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 12. Expectations/12.1. Expectation of Sums of R.V.
children.summary: This section, titled 'Expectation of Sums of R.V.', introduces theorems and examples for calculating the expectation of functions of random variables. It begins with Theorem 17, defining the expectation for joint probability mass functions (pmf) and probability density functions (pdf). Three examples follow: Example 1 calculates E[XY] using a discrete joint pmf table; Example 2 sets up a double integral for independent exponential random variables to find E[X²Y]; and Example 3 computes E[XY] and Var(Y) given a continuous joint pdf. The section then presents Theorem 18 on the linearity of expectation (E[X+Y] = E[X] + E[Y]) and provides its proof. Example 4 demonstrates that the expected value of the sample mean equals the population mean (μ). Finally, Theorem 19 states that for independent random variables X and Y, E[XY] = E[X]E[Y], followed by its proof and a generalization in Theorem 20.

children.title: 12.2. Covariance and Correlations.
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 12. Expectations/12.2. Covariance and Correlations.
children.summary: This section defines covariance and correlation for random variables. It provides the mathematical definitions, explains that covariance measures linear relationships (positive or negative), and lists its properties. The section then introduces the correlation coefficient as a standardized measure of linearity, detailing its range from -1 to 1 and what different values signify. A worked example demonstrates how to calculate the covariance, variance, and correlation coefficient for two random variables with a given joint probability density function.

sections.title: Chapter 13. Moment generating functions
sections.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 13. Moment generating functions

children.title: 13.1. Moment Generating Functions
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 13. Moment generating functions/13.1. Moment Generating Functions

children.title: Example3
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 13. Moment generating functions/13.1. Moment Generating Functions/Example3
children.summary: The section titled 'Example3' presents a problem involving two independent binomial random variables, X and Y. It demonstrates how to find the distribution of their sum (X + Y) by multiplying their respective moment generating functions (m.g.f.) and identifying the resulting distribution as another binomial distribution.

children.title: Example4
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 13. Moment generating functions/13.1. Moment Generating Functions/Example4
children.summary: The section presents Example 4, which involves a discrete random variable X defined by its moment generating function (m.g.f.). The example asks for the probability mass function (p.m.f.) of X and its expected value E[X]. The solution derives the p.m.f. coefficients directly from the m.g.f. terms and calculates the expectation by evaluating the first derivative of the m.g.f. at t=0.

children.title: Example5
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 13. Moment generating functions/13.1. Moment Generating Functions/Example5
children.summary: The section titled 'Example5' presents a problem where a random variable X has the moment generating function m_X(t) = (1 - 2t)^(-1/2). The solution demonstrates how to find the first and second moments of X by calculating the first derivative m'_X(t) and the second derivative m''_X(t), and then evaluating them at t=0. The calculated values are E[X] = 1 and E[X^2] = 3.

children.summary: The section titled 'Limit Laws' introduces the Central Limit Theorem (CLT), describing it as a key theorem in probability that explains why natural populations often exhibit bell-shaped curves. It defines i.i.d. (independent and identically distributed) random variables and presents Theorem 24, which states that the distribution of the standardized sum of i.i.d. variables with mean μ and variance σ² converges to the standard normal distribution Z as n approaches infinity. The text also notes the CLT's utility in approximating probabilities for sums of independent variables and mentions the use of ±0.5 continuity correction for discrete distributions. An example is provided involving rolling 10 fair dice to find the approximate probability that the sum is between 30 and 40.

children.title: 14.1. The Central Limit Theorem
children.path: Probability Theory Lecture Notes.pdf/Chapter 14. Limit Laws/14.1. The Central Limit Theorem
children.summary: This section introduces the Central Limit Theorem (CLT), a fundamental concept in probability that explains why many natural populations exhibit bell-shaped (normal) curves. It formally states that for independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables with mean μ and variance σ², the distribution of their standardized sum converges to the standard normal distribution as the sample size n approaches infinity. The text highlights the CLT's utility in approximating probabilities involving sums of i.i.d. variables and notes the use of the ±0.5 continuity correction when dealing with discrete distributions. Two examples are provided: one calculating the approximate probability of the sum of 10 fair dice rolls falling between 30 and 40, and another estimating the probability that an instructor can grade at least 25 exams within 450 minutes given the average grading time.
